lines.text: Daily routines provide structure and rhythm to our lives. Most people's day begins with waking up — some use an alarm clock, while others rise naturally with the sun. The morning routine typically includes getting out of bed, taking a shower or having a bath, brushing teeth, getting dressed, and eating breakfast. Commuting to work or school follows — by car, bus, train, bicycle, or on foot. The working day usually runs from nine to five, with a lunch break around midday. Afternoon tasks might include meetings, classes, errands, or household chores. The evening routine begins when people arrive home. Cooking dinner, eating together as a family, and doing the washing-up are common activities. Evening leisure varies widely: watching television, reading a book, exercising at a gym, scrolling through social media, or spending time with friends. Before bed, the nighttime routine includes changing into pyjamas, brushing teeth again, setting the alarm, and going to sleep. Some people are 'early birds' who thrive in the morning, while 'night owls' prefer staying up late. Weekend routines differ: sleeping in, running errands, visiting family, doing hobbies, or simply relaxing. Understanding daily routine vocabulary is essential for describing habits, making plans, and discussing lifestyle — common topics in English conversation and exams.

lines.text: The '9-to-5' phrase (from Dolly Parton's famous song) represents the standard working day in English-speaking countries. However, flexible working, remote work, and 'flexitime' are increasingly common. 'Work-life balance' is a key modern English term.

lines.text: In British workplaces, the 'tea break' is a sacred tradition — usually mid-morning and mid-afternoon. 'Put the kettle on' is an invitation to take a break. In offices, a 'coffee run' means going to buy coffee for the team.

lines.text: Meal names vary across English-speaking regions. 'Breakfast' is universal. 'Lunch' is the midday meal everywhere, but in northern England 'dinner' can mean lunch. 'Tea' can mean the evening meal (northern UK) or just the drink (southern UK).
